subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A substance with a high specific heat capacity will:
options: Heat up very quickly for a given energy input
Require more energy to change its temperature
questions.explain: A high specific heat capacity means more energy is needed to change the temperature of the substance.

questions.q: Heating a substance without changing its state increases its internal energy by:
options: Increasing the kinetic energy of its particles
Reducing the speed of the particles
questions.explain: Heating increases the kinetic energy of the particles, raising the temperature and internal energy.

questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explain: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Velocity has direction, so it is a vector; mass, temperature and speed are scalars (magnitude only).

questions.q: Changes of state such as melting and boiling are described as physical changes because:
options: The particles themselves are unchanged and the change can be reversed
Chemical bonds break to form new molecules
questions.explain: In a change of state the particles are the same substance, just rearranged, so it is reversible.

questions.q: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Which factor increases the thinking distance?
questions.explain: Thinking distance depends on reaction time, increased by tiredness, alcohol or distractions. Worn brakes, ice and bald tyres increase the braking distance instead.

questions.q: When ice melts to form water, what happens to the total mass?
questions.explain: Melting is a physical change: no particles are created or destroyed, so mass is conserved. The water has the same mass as the ice it came from.

questions.q: As you go deeper into a liquid, what happens to the pressure?
questions.explain: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth because there is a greater weight of fluid above pushing down (p = hρg).

questions.q: For a stable orbit, if a satellite moves to a larger orbital radius, what must happen to its speed?
options: It cannot stay in orbit at a larger radius
Its speed stays exactly the same
questions.explain: For a stable orbit at a given radius there is only one possible speed. A larger orbital radius requires a slower orbital speed; a smaller radius requires a faster speed.

questions.q: How do all electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum?
options: Only visible light can travel through a vacuum
All at the same speed (the speed of light)
At different speeds depending on frequency
They cannot travel through a vacuum
questions.explain: All EM waves are transverse and travel at the same speed (about 3 × 10⁸ m/s) through a vacuum. They differ in frequency and wavelength, not speed in a vacuum.

questions.q: Specific latent heat is the energy needed to:
options: Increase the pressure of a gas
Change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature
Raise the temperature of a substance
questions.explain: Specific latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature.

questions.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: Weight is measured in kilograms; mass in newtons
They are the same thing measured in different units
Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the gravitational force on it (N)
Mass changes with location; weight does not
questions.explain: Mass is the quantity of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, and is the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass, measured in newtons, and depends on the gravitational field strength.

questions.q: The internal energy of a substance is best described as:
options: The energy stored in the kinetic and potential energy of its particles
The energy needed to lift it
questions.explain: Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy stored in the particles of a substance.

questions.q: What does it mean if a spring is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality?
options: No more force is needed to stretch it
The extension is no longer directly proportional to the force
questions.explain: Beyond the limit of proportionality the force–extension graph is no longer a straight line, so extension is no longer directly proportional to force (and deformation may become inelastic).

questions.q: What happens to atmospheric pressure as you climb to a higher altitude?
questions.explain: As altitude increases there is less air above you, so the weight pressing down is smaller and atmospheric pressure decreases.

questions.q: Reducing the volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature will:
options: Change the gas into a liquid instantly
questions.explain: Squeezing the gas into a smaller volume means more frequent collisions with the walls, raising the pressure.

questions.q: A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m circular track, finishing where they started. What is their displacement?
questions.explain: Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish (a vector). Finishing at the start gives 0 m displacement, even though the distance travelled is 400 m.

questions.q: On a force–extension graph for a spring obeying Hooke's law, the line is:
options: A straight line through the origin
questions.explain: While a spring obeys Hooke's law, force is directly proportional to extension, so the force–extension graph is a straight line through the origin. The gradient equals the spring constant k.

questions.q: Why does light bend (refract) when it passes from air into glass?
options: Its speed changes, which changes its direction (unless it hits the boundary along the normal)
It speeds up in the glass
questions.explain: Refraction happens because the wave changes speed when it enters a different medium. Light slows down in glass; if it meets the boundary at an angle, this change of speed bends it toward the normal.

questions.q: In what direction do magnetic field lines around a bar magnet point?
options: From south pole to north pole outside the magnet
From north pole to south pole outside the magnet
questions.explain: By convention, magnetic field lines travel from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet. The direction is the direction of the force on a north pole.

questions.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid?
options: Spread out evenly with large gaps
Close together but able to flow past each other
Close together in a regular fixed pattern
questions.explain: In a solid the particles are packed closely in a regular arrangement and only vibrate about fixed positions.

questions.q: Which quantity is measured in a derived unit rather than an SI base unit?
questions.explain: A derived unit is built from base units. Speed (m/s) is metres divided by seconds, so it is derived. The second, metre and kilogram are SI base units.

questions.q: According to kinetic theory, the temperature of a gas is related to:
options: The average kinetic energy of its particles
The size of the container only
questions.explain: The higher the temperature, the greater the average kinetic energy of the gas particles.
